newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Greenpeace urges pressure on France over Mururoa.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace urges pressure on France over Mururoa.

text.p: Greenpeace on Friday called on the governments of New Zealand, Australia and the South Pacific to ask France to explain its plans for waste from the clean-up of Mururoa Atoll.
Greenpeace released photographs taken in the 1990s it said showed industrial waste from Hao military base near Mururoa being dumped at sea.
It said the photos gave credence to reports that waste from Mururoa would also be dumped at sea.

"Photos show huge piles of rubble and waste are being bulldozed into a barge and pulled out by military tug and the waste just deposited over the side into the water," Greenpeace New Zealand campaign co-ordinator Stephanie Mills told Reuters.
"You can see the atoll in the distance about five kilometres away."
The photos were given to Greenpeace in Tahiti by military personnel last year and were taken sometime in the 1990s, Mills said.
The waste included metal pipes, old tanks and construction rubble which could be contaminated by plutonium, she said.
"Hao was an assembly site for nuclear weapons and had a radiation laboratory, so the question is: 'was any of this dumped in the sea?'"
New Zealand and Australia spearheaded global protests against the six French nuclear tests at Mururoa last year.
France has ruled out future testing and signed the Rarotonga Treaty making the South Pacific a nuclear-free zone. It is cleaning up the atoll and will abandon it.

"We will depart after returning Mururoa to its natural state, leaving the atoll as we found it when we arrived 30 years ago," General Michel Boileau, the French military officer responsible for the clean-up, told reporters allowed a rare glimpse of the remote and secret base on Thursday.
General Boileau said about 1,000 workers were involved in the demolition which would be completed in mid-1998.
"But there are no independent observers watching the clean-up so it is very hard to ascertain what is going on," Mills said.
"We don't know what is being dumped and where it is being dumped," she said.
"A superficial clean-up from deconstructing buildings and pushing waste into the ocean does not deal with the long-term contamination of the atoll."
